Iranian officials gloat as US voters deal blow to Trump

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power.

IRAN: Iran's government savoured the stinging rebuke delivered to Donald Trump in the midterm elections, declaring voters had rejected the war launched by the US president even as Tehran remained on high alert for the possibility of renewed strikes. "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, posted on X on Wednesday (Nov 4), adding that Washington should not ignore public opinion by attacking his country again. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power, warning against "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the US . "The US sees the end of its hegemony as distant; we see it as near," he added. OLD FOES

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and Ho us e in Tuesday's election , with victories in Republican strongholds underscoring deep fr us tration with Trump 's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war that drove up gas prices. In Iran, a news outlet run by the judiciary shared a joke circulating on X that " Trump failed at regime change in Iran but he succeeded in Texas", a reference to the southern state where a Democrat won a Senate race for the first time in decades. But two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that while Iranian leaders welcomed the Democrats’ victory, Tehran was concerned that Trump could seek to compensate for it with a military strike, and remained on high alert. Iran's leaders have long regarded the United States as their main enemy, referring to it as "the Great Satan". At a state-organised rally on Wednesday commemorating the student takeover of the US embassy in Tehran during the 1979 Islamic revolution, demonstrators voiced triumph at an election they linked to Iran's success in surviving months of US attacks. "The fact that the might of these warmongering Republicans has been broken, something unprecedented in human history, means that from now on we will see the real war unfolding inside the US Senate and among American officials ," said one, giving only his family name of Nazari.

Pictures of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on a dartboard during the 47th anniversary of the US expulsion from Iran, in Tehran, Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: West Asia News Agency via REUTERS/Majid Asgaripour)

Mediators have intensified efforts to end the war amid fears it could reignite after the election , with Trump on Tuesday declining to rule out a resumption of combat operations after the vote and Iran planning wider retaliation if war resumes. The US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28, and Iran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. Conflict also erupted in Lebanon between Iran-backed Hezbollah and Israel, and more recently spread to Yemen, from where the Iran-aligned Houthis have struck energy facilities, airports and other targets in Saudi Arabia. Global oil and gas prices have shot up with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted after Tehran declared it closed, while the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, hitting Iran's economy hard. "IRAN'S SHADOW OVER US ELECTIONS" Ahead of the US election, senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was deliberately prolonging talks with the US to weaken Trump politically ahead of the vote. Some news outlets played on the timing of the election on the anniversary of the embassy seizure, when radical students cemented Iran's toppling of the US -backed Shah by storming the embassy and holding 52 Americans hostage there for 444 days. Major Iranian newspaper Hamshahri linked the events with a front-page image showing Trump blindfolded with his head bowed. With a headline declaring "Iran's shadow over US elections", it said Washington had been "47 years Iran's captive: from the capture of the spies' nest ( US embassy) to the November 2026 US Congress elections". The Iran war has been unpopular among Americans since it began, and blaming the war for driving up costs was a foc us of the Democrats' election campaign. Khamenei's message signalled that Tehran had no intention of showing flexibility on its demands for lasting control over the Strait of Hormuz or conditions to end the conflict. "The consequences of ( US ) miscalculations and arrogant del us ions have manifested as a heavy burden of costs, borne by the American people and the puppet regimes subservient to the US government," he said. Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war that is now in its ninth month. "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, referring to the election result. The conservative Iranian newspaper Jam-e Jam declared the election result "The twilight of Trump ism".

Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms' win marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground.

WASHINGTON: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won Georgia’s race for governor on Tuesday (Nov 3), becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US state and delivering Democrats a victory in one of the nation's most closely divided political battlegrounds. The former Atlanta mayor, who will also be the first female governor of the state, defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson, according to US media projections. She succeeds Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who is leaving office after serving two consecutive terms. Bottoms, 56, also previously served as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement.

Former US President Barack Obama speaks as Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms listen during a rally ahead of the midterm elections in Morrow, Georgia, US on Oct 28, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Edgar Su)

The victory marked a new milestone for Black women in American politics, who have long been a core base within the Democratic Party but remain underrepresented in the nation’s highest elected offices. The same evening, Stacey Plaskett was elected governor of the US Virgin Islands, a US territory, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US jurisdiction.

Bottoms' win also marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground. Republicans had controlled the governor’s office for more than two decades. Jackson, the billionaire founder of healthcare staffing company Jackson Healthcare, cast himself as a political outsider and campaigned on tax cuts, public safety and reducing government regulation. Bottoms’ victory comes eight years after fellow Democrat Stacey Abrams became the first Black woman nominated for governor by a major US political party. Abrams lost governor's races in Georgia in 2018 and 2022, but her campaigns helped to build a multigenerational, multiracial coalition that boosted Democratic turnout, helped elect two Democratic US senators and delivered Georgia’s electoral votes to a Democratic presidential candidate for the first time in decades.

COPENHAGEN: Greenland's parliament on Tuesday (Nov 3) ratified the Arctic island's security agreement struck earlier this year with US President Donald Trump, although some opposition party members questioned the deal's economic value. The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September, aimed at ending tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory. The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. A majority of lawmakers had already signalled support for the deal in a first debate last month.

Tuesday's vote was 16 in favour and none against, with seven abstentions. The White House in January said Trump was discussing options for acquiring Greenland, including potential use of the US military, alarming governments in Europe and triggering intense diplomatic efforts to calm the situation. Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said on Tuesday that ratification of the deal was an important step for the island. "We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted," Egede told lawmakers in Nuuk shortly before the vote. Opposition party Naleraq, the most prominent political voice for Greenland's independence, questioned the deal's economic value during the debate. "We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement," Naleraq chair Pele Broberg said. The Danish parliament is due to give the bill a first reading on Nov 11, followed by a second reading and a vote on Nov 19. The executive agreement will enter into force once Denmark and Greenland have ratified it, and does not require approval from the US Senate.

Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump

Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled US President Donald Trump to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats.

Supporters celebrate Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's victory in the midterm elections, at the Democratic Election Night rally, in Columbus, Ohio, US, on Nov 3, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Shannon Stapleton)

FAST

WASHINGTON: Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House on Tuesday (Nov 3), scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump. Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fuelled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump's stewardship of the country . Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago. In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate. And in Texas, the biggest Republican state, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning a Senate seat and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott.

The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump.

US Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) waves to supporters during an election night rally after winning reelection in the US midterm elections, in Atlanta, Georgia on Nov 3, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Carlos Barria)

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. "There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America," said Chuck Schumer, the party's Senate minority leader. "Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver." Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. But the new balance of power in Washington may accelerate his lame-duck status, as attention turns toward the 2028 presidential race and potential successors begin competing for political influence in a post-Trump world. Despite worries from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the election results , as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome, congratulating Democrats in an interview with Fox News. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any "insane" bills they passed.

Related:

Trump says will accept results of US midterm election, NYT reports

Commentary: What to watch for in the US midterm elections

DEMOCRATIC WAVE Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump's tariff policy and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House. Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats over culture war issues such as transgender rights while portraying their opponents as radical and extreme. But in poll after poll, voters made it clear they were far more concerned with pocketbook issues. The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in all but a handful of the approximately 1,700 counties where most votes had been counted on Tuesday night, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today. Democrats made gains in the richest counties and the poorest; in counties where more people have college degrees and where fewer do. Democrats' advances were particularly sharp in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

Supporters celebrate outside the venue for the election night rally of Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during the US midterm elections in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Dieu-Nalio Chery)

In Seward County, Kansas, home to one of America's biggest beef processing plants and where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic, Democrat Adam Hamilton led incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 13 points, two years after Trump won the county by 39 points. Democrats ran the table in the House races thought to be especially competitive, winning all 20 of the contests decided so far. Meanwhile, an unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make them more favourable largely failed, with Democrats hanging on to most of the targeted seats. Midterm elections are typically seen as a referendum on the sitting president, and Trump did little to disabuse voters of that notion. In the campaign's final weeks, he held dozens of rallies, telling supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot". He also intervened in several races to ensure his preferred candidates reached the ballot, despite concerns from some Republicans that his choices carried significant liabilities. In Texas, Trump backed Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden state attorney general, over the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. In South Carolina, the president anointed Darline Graham, a political neophyte, after her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly earlier this year. Both candidates lost. But even candidates who sought to distance themselves from Trump were unable to escape voters' wrath. In Maine, Republican incumbent Susan Collins had her 30-year Senate career end on Tuesday, despite emphasising her willingness to break with the president during the campaign. Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open Senate seat on Tuesday, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He defeated Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, who entered the race with Trump's backing and sought to falsely portray El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American born in Michigan, as a religious extremist. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed told cheering supporters on Tuesday night, referring to Rogers.

Related:

Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state

Historic leadership firsts for minorities across US in midterm vote

Competitive Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska had yet to be called early on Wednesday. On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter." VOTERS REBUKE TRUMP According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed. In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president. "In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia told supporters at a victory party. The night included several historic firsts for both parties. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, while Byron Donalds won Florida's gubernatorial race to become the first Black Republican governor in the US. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino governor.

Related:

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

Source: Reuters/bg

DUBAI: Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iran ian official told Reuters on Tuesday (Nov 3), while mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to bridge differences and avert a renewed escalation after the US midterm elections . Overnight, the United States carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran 's Qeshm island targeting surface-to-air missiles us ed against US assets, a US official said. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations. US President Donald Trump on Tuesday renewed threats of possible military action, telling Fox News Channel: "I'm not looking to ... kill lots of people. If we have to , we'll have to." Qatar has intensified mediation efforts amid fears the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after Tuesday's midterms.

"Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington," the senior Iran ian official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks on a version of a draft US - Iran deal disc us sed over the past eight days. "Tehran's conditions m us t be met if the US wants Hormuz reopened," the Iran ian official cautioned, referring to Iran ian demands including waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iran ian funds. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran 's Supreme National Security Council, later said the US response to Iran ian demands "was not convincing", adding that Washington "m us t fully and explicitly address Iran 's seven conditions and act upon them". "Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened," he wrote on X.

"WE CANNOT LOSE HOPE" On Monday, Trump raised doubts about whether he would follow through on a threatened resumption of military strikes against Iran and said a deal with Tehran could happen. Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said both the United States and Iran were reviewing proposals put forward by mediators. While the Qatari team that travelled to Tehran had returned to Doha, talks were continuing. "There are intensive joint regional efforts underway to avoid escalation," he told a news briefing, adding that Qatar remained hopeful a deal could still be reached to pave the way for future negotiations. "If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations ... and as a mediator, we cannot lose hope," he said. An official briefed on the talks said feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within the next 36 hours.

Related:

US signals progress in talks with Iran to avert renewed war

"FORCEFUL RESPONSE" The senior Iran ian official said Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands" and that nuclear talks could begin only after Iran 's conditions were met. Tehran would respond forcefully, in the region and beyond, to US strikes, the official added. Oil prices rose about 1.3 per cent, having dropped more than 7 per cent the previo us day on hopes diplomacy was progressing. Iran 's Revolutionary Guards said they downed a US MQ-9 drone and two Lucas drones in the skies near the Strait of Hormuz. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after Tehran had delivered what he described as a "strong and rational response". "The enemy seeks to force the Iran ian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said. He added that Tehran's response to any US miscalculation would be unpredictable and unconstrained by geography. The head of Iran 's armed forces general staff, Ali Abdollahi, said Iran 's military was updating target lists that included US and Israeli assets and would respond immediately to any threat. Since Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei ordered the armed forces last week to respond immediately and without "geographic limits" to any enemy threat, Iran ian officials and media have increasingly raised the prospect of striking bases beyond the region us ed to launch attacks on Iran . Hardline newspaper Kayhan said on Tuesday that US facilities in Britain, Italy, Greece, Romania, Albania and Cypr us could be targeted in the event of renewed war.

IRAN IAN-SAUDI TALKS Alongside indirect exchanges between Tehran and Washington, regional powers are pursuing diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation. The conflict has also widened, with Yemen's Iran -aligned Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi Arabia. Iran ian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Tuesday that talks with Saudi Arabia were continuing to seek new regional security arrangements that would exclude foreign military involvement. Last week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iran ian counterparts in Tehran, the first such high-level contacts since Aug us t.

MADRID: Services on the Madrid-Seville rail line will be reduced after last week's crash until Spain's Railway Safety Agency reviews the line's safety system and the government completes the delayed rollout of the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS), Transport Minister Oscar Puente told reporters on Tuesday (Nov 3). The crash killed 69 people near the town of Urda in central Spain. Another in January , involving the same companies on the same line, killed 46. Several trains were automatically stopped last Wednesday due to the failure of a signalling system, after which central controllers in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorised to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Puente. Investigators estimated an impact speed of 160 to 200 kph (100 to 125 mph).

TRANSPORT MINISTER TO FACE LAWMAKERS Puente, who has ruled out resigning , was to face questions from lawmakers at 5pm local time over his handling of Europe's worst train crash since 2013, as the leftist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, seeking re-election on Nov 29, approved an emergency aid package for victims and their families. It has promised to double compulsory passenger insurance payouts for crash victims, speed up compensation payments and improve temporary incapacity cover. Puente presented new safety measures, including a 40 kph (25 mph) speed limit when relying on a driver to spot obstacles ahead if a signal system fails, hiring more staff and improving conditions in rail control centres. The government will also push for a faster rollout of the standardised ERTMS for safety and signalling across its network. Its implementation is behind schedule on the line where the accidents occurred, government contracts show. In addition, in what Puente said would be a world first, the railway system will introduce an AI agent to "detect anomalies and monitor conversations" between train drivers and controllers to minimise the likelihood of human error. "We are not aware of any other railway system that uses this type of mechanism or technology. We will be the first to go down this path," Puente said, adding that Spain would also create a real-time digital model of the network.
